title: Does the Board follow the district’s own supervisor?
question: When a land-use matter names a district, how does that district’s supervisor vote, and how often do the other ten vote the same way?
finding: On 575 full-Board roll calls on matters whose title names a district (2015 to November 2026), the other members cast 97.9% of their votes the same way as that district’s supervisor, though 95.0% of all 1,618 land-use roll calls had no dissent at all. In the 32 divided ones the district supervisor was on the winning side 21 times (65.6%), against 80.3% for colleagues on the same votes.
how: Matters are the 1,872 land-use files in the Board’s legislative system for 2015-2026. A district is taken from the title where it prints “(District N)” - mostly appeals and liquor-licence findings - and carried from an appeal’s hearing file to its sibling motions. One vote printed on several sibling files is counted once. The district supervisor is the member holding that seat on the day of the vote. “Other members’ votes the same” counts each aye or no cast by the other members. A divided roll call has at least one aye and one no. All 33 members named in the roll calls could be placed in a district seat from files: the City’s district-boundary files (which carry the sitting supervisor’s name), the Department of Elections’ Statement of the Vote (who stood in which district), a roll call that prints a district as vacant, and succession (a seat passes from the member who leaves the roll call to the one who joins). The method used for each member is in this file’s notes.
limits: Voting with the district supervisor is what near-unanimous voting produces by itself: most of these roll calls had no dissent at all, so agreement says little about deference. The divided roll calls are few, and the comparison there is with colleagues on the same votes, not with a rule. A unanimous result can also follow a disagreement settled before the vote, or a motion already shaped to the district supervisor’s wish; the roll call cannot show either. Titles print a district for appeals and liquor licences but rarely for rezonings, so this covers only part of land-use business. A difference between areas, or between groups of cases, is not proof of bias. Areas differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply, object or appeal at all.
